questions.question: A packet traverses a router. The router INSPECTS the destination IP address, performs a longest-prefix-match against its routing table, and forwards out the egress interface. This decision happens at exactly ONE of the OSI layers — the one that defines LOGICAL (IP) addresses and routing between networks. Which layer?
options: Layer 4 Transport — handles ports and TCP/UDP segments, not logical addressing
Layer 2 Data Link — handles MAC addresses + frames within one segment, not routing between networks
Layer 1 Physical — bits on the wire, not logical addressing
Layer 3 Network — logical addressing (IP) + inter-network routing
questions.explanation: Layer 3 (Network) handles logical addressing (IP addresses) and routing between networks. Layer 2 handles MAC addressing within a network segment.

questions.question: A developer wants to test a local web server WITHOUT putting it on any network. Operating systems reserve a special IPv4 address that always loops back to the local host's stack. Connecting to it tests the network-stack and the application without leaving the machine. Which IPv4 address?
options: 10.0.0.1 — a private-range address (RFC 1918), not the loopback
172.16.0.1 — another private-range address (RFC 1918), not loopback
192.168.0.1 — another private-range address (RFC 1918), not loopback
questions.explanation: 127.0.0.1 (the 127.0.0.0/8 range) is the IPv4 loopback address used to test local TCP/IP stack. Pinging it tests the NIC driver without sending traffic on the network.

questions.question: A user types `https://news.example.com` in their browser. Before the HTTPS request can be sent, the client must resolve that human-readable name to a routable IP address. The resolver queries authoritative servers up the hierarchy (root → .com → example.com → news). Which protocol provides this name-to-IP resolution?
options: DNS
BGP — inter-AS routing, not name resolution
HTTPS — the secure transport for the page request, not the prior name resolution
DHCP — leases IP / mask / gateway / DNS-server to LAN clients, not name resolution
questions.explanation: DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names (e.g., google.com) into IP addresses. It uses a hierarchical distributed database.

questions.question: A wireless engineer is replacing a legacy 802.11g network. The replacement standard must support DUAL-BAND operation (both the original 2.4 GHz channel space AND the newer 5 GHz space) and offer MIMO. Which IEEE 802.11 amendment was the FIRST to operate on BOTH 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz?
options: 802.11a — 5 GHz only
802.11g — 2.4 GHz only
802.11b — 2.4 GHz only
questions.explanation: 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4) operates on both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz. 802.11a and 802.11ac use 5 GHz only. 802.11b and 802.11g use 2.4 GHz only.

questions.question: An enterprise has one physical switch carrying traffic for SALES, FINANCE, and ENGINEERING. Each team's broadcast traffic should be isolated; finance frames must NOT leak to sales or engineering ports. A switch feature partitions the broadcast domain logically. What is this feature?
options: Virtual Link between two remote offices — wrong term
Variable Length Address Network — wrong; describes CIDR/VLSM
Virtual LAN (VLAN)
Very Large Area Network — wrong term
questions.explanation: VLANs logically segment a single physical switch into multiple broadcast domains, improving security, performance, and network management without requiring separate hardware.

questions.question: An IPv4 interface is configured `192.168.10.50 255.255.255.0`. The mask determines which BITS of the address identify the NETWORK portion (255.255.255 = first 24 bits) versus the HOST portion (.0 = last 8 bits) — letting the host decide whether a destination is on the same subnet (ARP) or off-net (default gateway). What does the subnet mask do?
options: Encrypts specific bits of the IP address to protect traffic between hosts on the same network segment
Prevents broadcast storms by allowing switches to identify which portion of the IP address belongs to which network segment
Routes packets between VLANs by helping the router identify which network and host portion of the address to forward to the next hop
Defines which bits of the IP identify the NETWORK vs the HOST portion
questions.explanation: A subnet mask defines the boundary between the network portion and host portion of an IP address. Devices in the same subnet can communicate directly; others require a router.

questions.question: A host on a /24 LAN wants to send a packet to 192.168.1.50. Its routing table says 'on-link' so the destination is on the same broadcast segment. The host has the IP but needs the destination's MAC address to build the L2 frame. Which protocol resolves IP→MAC on a LAN?
options: DHCP — leases IPs, not L2 resolution
ARP
RARP — older MAC-to-IP (reverse of ARP), now obsolete
NDP — IPv6 neighbour discovery, not IPv4 ARP
questions.explanation: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) dynamically maps a known IPv4 address to an unknown MAC address by broadcasting an ARP request on the local network.

questions.question: A home / branch office has 200 LAN hosts with RFC1918 private IPs (192.168.0.0/24). They share ONE public IP issued by the ISP. The router maps each outbound flow's private source IP + port to its public IP + a unique port. Replies are translated back. What does this technology do?
options: Assigns dynamic IPs via DHCP — different function
Segments switches into VLANs — different function (L2 isolation)
Encrypts traffic in transit — separate, encryption concern
NAT/PAT
questions.explanation: NAT (Network Address Translation) allows multiple devices with private IPs to share one or more public IPs, conserving IPv4 addresses and providing a layer of security.

questions.question: A cable certifier reports `Split Pair` on a Cat6 patch cable. The fault is when wires from DIFFERENT twisted pairs (e.g., pair 1 white/blue and pair 2 white/orange) are swapped at the RJ-45 termination. Continuity passes end-to-end (1↔1, 2↔2, …) but crosstalk is terrible. What is the fault?
options: Cable length exceeds 100 m — a different fault class reported as attenuation, not as a split pair wiring error
Both ends terminated to T568B — correct and matching termination; not a split pair or wiring fault
Damaged shielding — a physical fault causing EMI susceptibility but not a split pair wiring error
Split Pair
questions.explanation: A split pair occurs when wires from different twisted pairs are crossed at termination. The cable still passes basic continuity tests but suffers heavy near-end crosstalk, causing intermittent throughput and CRC errors.

questions.question: An email server sends outbound mail to another SMTP server using the LEGACY plaintext mail-transfer port. (Modern submission uses 587/465 instead.) Which TCP port is the original SMTP server-to-server port?
options: TCP 110 — POP3 mail-retrieval protocol for clients fetching mail from a server; not a mail-transfer port
TCP 143 — IMAP mail-retrieval protocol used by clients accessing a mail server; not a server-to-server transfer port
TCP 25 — original SMTP server-to-server mail transfer
TCP 587 — the modern SMTP message-submission port used by mail clients authenticating to a mail server; not the original server-to-server relay port
questions.explanation: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) uses port 25 for server-to-server email relay. Port 587 is used for authenticated client-to-server submission. Port 110 is POP3, 143 is IMAP.

questions.question: An installer is running Cat6 UTP from the IDF to user desks. The Ethernet standard caps the run length so end-to-end signal integrity stays within spec at 1 Gbps / 10 Gbps. What is the MAXIMUM end-to-end cable length for Cat5e/Cat6 UTP Ethernet?
options: 500 m — far above the spec; signal would degrade well before
100 m total (90 m horizontal + 10 m patch cords)
185 m — that's the limit for 10BASE2 thinnet coax, not UTP
50 m — too short; the spec is 100 m
questions.explanation: The maximum segment length for 10BASE-T, 100BASE-TX, and 1000BASE-T over UTP (Cat5e/Cat6) is 100 meters (328 feet), including patch cables.

questions.question: An attacker connects a laptop to a switch port and sends thousands of frames with RANDOM source MAC addresses. The switch's CAM table fills past capacity, evicts legitimate entries, and starts FLOODING unknown-destination frames out every port (like a hub) — letting the attacker sniff all traffic. Which attack is this?
options: STP attack — an attacker sends superior BPDUs to win the root bridge election; the goal is topology manipulation, not CAM-table flooding
MAC flooding (CAM-table overflow)
ARP poisoning — an attacker sends gratuitous ARP replies to poison neighbour caches and redirect traffic; it does not flood the MAC address table
VLAN hopping — an attacker escapes the assigned VLAN via tag manipulation or DTP negotiation; it does not cause CAM-table overflow flooding
questions.explanation: MAC flooding attacks overwhelm a switch's CAM (Content Addressable Memory) table. When full, the switch broadcasts all frames, allowing an attacker to capture traffic.

questions.question: An IGP advertises ENTIRE routing table to neighbours every 30 seconds and uses HOP COUNT (max 15) as its metric. Loop-prevention is via split-horizon + route-poisoning. The algorithm behind it is Bellman-Ford. Which protocol fits this description?
options: OSPF — link-state, Dijkstra/SPF, not Bellman-Ford
EIGRP — advanced distance-vector with DUAL, not Bellman-Ford
RIP
BGP — path-vector, uses best-path selection, not Bellman-Ford
questions.explanation: RIP (Routing Information Protocol) uses the Bellman-Ford algorithm and hop count as its metric. OSPF uses Dijkstra's SPF algorithm, EIGRP uses DUAL.

questions.question: An organisation places its public web server, mail relay, and DNS resolver into a SEPARATE network segment between the public internet (untrusted) and the internal LAN (trusted). Inbound internet traffic terminates in that segment; the segment cannot freely reach LAN. What is this segment called?
options: A firewall ACL — a rule that filters traffic crossing an interface; it is a configuration object, not a separate network segment
DMZ (Demilitarised Zone) / perimeter network
Native VLAN — the VLAN that carries untagged frames on an 802.1Q trunk; a VLAN assignment concept, not a separate network segment between two zones
VPN tunnel endpoint — a device that terminates encrypted tunnels; a connectivity mechanism, not a physically separate network segment
questions.explanation: A DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) is a network segment that sits between the internet and the internal LAN, hosting publicly accessible servers (web, mail) while protecting the internal network.

questions.question: Voice and video traffic on a network must be PRIORITISED over bulk file copies. Routers and switches mark, classify, queue, and schedule traffic to give latency-sensitive flows lower jitter and lower drop. Which networking discipline is this?
options: Quality of Servers — not a networking discipline
Queue of Sessions — not a real metric
Quantity of Subnets — irrelevant concept
Quality of Service (QoS)
questions.explanation: QoS (Quality of Service) mechanisms prioritize certain types of traffic (VoIP, video conferencing) over others (file downloads) to ensure acceptable performance for time-sensitive applications.

questions.question: An IPv6 host comes up on a fresh interface. Even with NO RA / DHCPv6 received, it immediately has a usable address with prefix FE80::/10 that is scoped to ONE link — never routed off-segment. Which address category is this?
options: Unique Local — FC00::/7, routable within an org (organisation-scoped)
Multicast — FF::/8, not the link-local
Global Unicast — 2000::/3, globally routable, opposite scope
Link-Local
questions.explanation: Link-local addresses (FE80::/10) are automatically assigned to every IPv6 interface and are only valid on the local link. They are never routed beyond the local segment.

questions.question: A legacy device floods every received frame out of every other port — every collision domain is shared, full duplex impossible. Its replacement learns MAC addresses, builds a CAM table, and forwards frames only to the port where the destination MAC was learned (or floods broadcasts/unknowns). Which devices are these?
options: A hub forwards frames faster than a switch because it has no MAC learning overhead — false; switches forward more efficiently using the CAM table
There is no functional difference between a hub and a switch — false; a hub floods every frame out every port while a switch forwards frames only to the learned destination port
Hub = floods every frame out every port (L1)
Switch is L1, hub is L2 — reversed; hub=L1, switch=L2
questions.explanation: Hubs (Layer 1) broadcast every received frame out all other ports, creating one collision domain. Switches (Layer 2) learn source MAC addresses into a CAM table and forward frames only to the destination port, eliminating collisions on switched links.

questions.question: An admin must manage a remote switch's CLI over the network. The protocol must (a) authenticate the user, (b) encrypt the session, (c) protect against MITM, (d) be the standard replacement for Telnet. Which protocol?
options: FTP — file-transfer protocol that uses plaintext credentials; not an encrypted CLI session standard or a Telnet replacement
SNMPv1 — a network-management protocol with plaintext community strings; not an interactive encrypted CLI session and not the standard Telnet replacement
Telnet — plaintext interactive CLI protocol with no encryption; the legacy protocol that SSH was designed to replace as the standard secure CLI
SSH — authenticated, encrypted CLI session; standard Telnet replacement
questions.explanation: SSH (Secure Shell) provides encrypted remote access for device management, replacing the insecure Telnet. SSH uses port 22 and provides authentication and encryption.

questions.question: A user reports: pinging 8.8.8.8 works fine, but pinging google.com returns 'unable to resolve'. The L3 path is healthy — the problem is the name-to-IP translation. Which component is failing?
options: DNS — server is unreachable, slow, or misconfigured on the client (works by IP, fails by name)
Default gateway — if this were the issue, name lookups AND IP connectivity would both fail; the scenario confirms IP-level reachability works
Local firewall blocking ICMP — would prevent ping by IP as well as by name; the IP ping succeeds in this scenario
Duplicate IP conflict — a different fault class that disrupts IP-level reachability, not just name resolution
questions.explanation: If ping by IP works but hostname fails, name resolution is the issue. The DNS server may be unreachable, the wrong DNS server is configured, or the hostname doesn't exist in DNS.

questions.question: An attacker connects an unauthorised DHCP server to a corporate LAN. The rogue server responds faster than the legitimate one, handing clients a leased IP, a malicious DEFAULT GATEWAY (the attacker), and a malicious DNS. The attacker now has a MITM position. What is this attack called?
options: Two legitimate DHCP servers configured with overlapping scopes — an operator error, not a rogue or unauthorised server providing a malicious gateway
The authorised DHCP server crashed — an availability failure; no rogue server is involved and clients simply fail to renew
Rogue DHCP server — unauthorised DHCP server hands out wrong gateway/DNS to enable a man-in-the-middle
DHCP starvation — an attacker floods the pool with spoofed MACs to exhaust the authorised server, often used alongside a rogue server attack but distinct
questions.explanation: A rogue DHCP server responds to client requests before the legitimate server, providing a malicious default gateway (attacker's device) to intercept traffic — a man-in-the-middle attack.

questions.question: A campus has Cisco, HP, and Juniper switches. The team wants ONE Layer-2 neighbour discovery protocol that all three vendors implement natively. It's defined by IEEE and exchanges device-identity TLVs. Which protocol matches?
options: CDP (Cisco Discovery Protocol) — a Cisco-proprietary Layer-2 neighbour-discovery protocol; HP and Juniper switches do not natively implement CDP
LLDP runs only on routers and access points, not on switches — false; LLDP (IEEE 802.1AB) runs on switches, routers, access points, and IP phones across all vendors
LLDP = IEEE 802.1AB vendor-neutral neighbour discovery; works between Cisco, HP, Juniper, Arista, etc.
LLDP and CDP are different names for the same IEEE protocol — false; they are different protocols with different OUIs, TLV sets, and standardisation bodies
questions.explanation: LLDP (IEEE 802.1AB) is the open-standard equivalent of Cisco's CDP. Both advertise device capabilities, port info, and IP addresses at Layer 2. Most modern multi-vendor environments use LLDP.

questions.question: A network monitoring system polls routers, switches, and firewalls every 60 s for interface byte counters, CPU, memory, environment sensors. It can also SET variables (with the right community / user). Communication is UDP 161 (polls) / UDP 162 (traps). Which protocol?
options: A VPN tunnel protocol — not management
SNMP
SSH — remote-shell protocol, not bulk metric polling
RIP — distance-vector routing protocol, not management
questions.explanation: SNMP (v1, v2c, v3) lets a Network Management System poll device counters (CPU, interfaces, errors) and push configuration. Always prefer SNMPv3 — it adds authentication and encryption to the management plane.

questions.question: Before going live, an ops team measures over two weeks the normal range of: per-link utilisation, latency between key endpoints, error counters, and application response time. They store this as a reference. Months later they compare CURRENT measurements against the reference to detect deviation. What's this reference called?
options: Network baseline
SLA floor — the contractual minimum, not the measured normal
Default vendor configuration — what's shipped, not what's measured
Factory-reset template — bootstrap config, not performance
questions.explanation: A baseline captures normal performance (bandwidth utilization, latency, error rates, CPU). When issues arise, comparing current metrics against the baseline quickly identifies anomalies.

questions.question: A campus with mixed Cisco + HP + Juniper routers needs FIRST-HOP REDUNDANCY (default-gateway HA) using an OPEN-standard protocol that every vendor implements natively. The protocol elects a virtual IP and virtual MAC across two or more routers in active/standby. Which?
options: VRRP
HSRP — Cisco proprietary, no Juniper/HP support
GLBP — Cisco proprietary with load balancing
EIGRP — routing protocol, not first-hop redundancy
questions.explanation: VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) is the IEEE standard for default gateway redundancy — vendor neutral. HSRP and GLBP are Cisco-proprietary. All use a virtual IP/MAC shared among routers.

questions.question: A service-provider backbone forwards customer packets using a SHORT (20-bit) label stack pushed onto each packet at the ingress PE, swapped at every P-router, and popped at the egress PE. No IP routing lookup happens inside the core — only label-based forwarding. Which technology?
options: A BGP extension used in SP backbones that forwards packets using community attributes without requiring a label lookup — incorrect; MPLS label lookups replace IP route lookups in the core
Wireless WPA3 encryption applied in backbone core segments so that forwarding decisions are encrypted — unrelated to label switching or IP lookup replacement
MPLS — Multiprotocol Label Switching; forwards by short labels, no IP-lookup in the core
A DSCP QoS marking scheme applied in the core that forwards short-priority packets on faster paths — false; DSCP marks IP headers for QoS but does not replace IP lookup with label forwarding
questions.explanation: MPLS assigns short labels to packets at ingress. Core routers forward based on labels (not IP lookups) — much faster. Widely used by ISPs for VPNs, Traffic Engineering, and connecting enterprise sites.

questions.question: A 1 G UTP link connecting a server NIC to a switch is locked to '1000-full' on both sides. There is no shared media; transmit and receive use separate pair sets simultaneously. Performance benchmarks show no collisions. Which Ethernet mode is this and how does it differ from the alternative?
options: Half-duplex can transmit and receive simultaneously faster than full-duplex on dedicated pair sets — false; half-duplex can only send OR receive at a time on shared media
Half-duplex = send OR receive at a time (shared media + CSMA/CD with hubs)
Full-duplex is a legacy backward-compatibility mode used only when older hubs cannot transmit and receive simultaneously — false; full-duplex is the modern default for switched Ethernet
Half-duplex and full-duplex transmit and receive at identical throughput because each shares the same wire pairs — false; half-duplex shares media and is limited by CSMA/CD collisions
questions.explanation: Modern switched Ethernet uses full-duplex — simultaneous TX/RX, no collisions, no CSMA/CD needed. Half-duplex shares the medium — only one device transmits at a time using CSMA/CD collision avoidance.

questions.question: A slow receiver (10/100 link, full buffer) is being blasted by a fast sender (1 G link). To prevent buffer overrun, a layer mechanism lets the receiver signal: 'pause, my buffer is full'. The sender slows down for a window. Which mechanism is this?
options: Inter-VLAN routing weight — different concept
Switch unknown-unicast filtering — different feature
Flow control
STP port state machine — different concept
questions.explanation: Flow control prevents buffer overflow at the receiver. Ethernet uses PAUSE frames (802.3x) in full-duplex. TCP uses its sliding window mechanism for end-to-end flow control.

questions.question: An Ethernet frame has a payload size limit. Standard Ethernet uses 1500 bytes; some storage/iSCSI deployments use 9000-byte jumbo frames. The acronym is the same — the value differs. What does the acronym mean and what is the STANDARD Ethernet value?
options: MTU = Maximum Transmission Unit; standard Ethernet MTU = 1500 bytes (excluding the 14-byte L2 header)
MTU stands for Maximum Token Unit — the legacy Token Ring framing unit; standard Ethernet does not use Token Ring framing or that acronym
MTU stands for Minimum Transmission Unit and the standard value is 64 bytes — false; the standard Ethernet minimum frame size is 64 bytes but that is a floor, not the MTU ceiling
MTU stands for Maximum Transfer Unit and the standard value is 9000 bytes — semantically similar wording but 9000 bytes is the jumbo frame size, not the standard 1500-byte Ethernet MTU
questions.explanation: MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) is the largest payload that fits in one Layer 2 frame without fragmentation. Standard Ethernet is 1500 bytes; jumbo frames extend this to 9000 bytes for storage and HPC workloads. An MTU mismatch in the path causes silent drops when DF is set.

questions.question: A distance-vector routing protocol prevents one specific loop pattern by REFUSING to advertise a route back out the interface from which the route was learned. The rule alone doesn't catch all loops but combined with route-poisoning and hold-down it covers most. What is this rule called?
options: Splitting one broadcast domain into halves — that's L2 segmentation, unrelated
Area route summarisation — OSPF / EIGRP feature, different
Update fragmentation — not a real protocol mechanism
Split horizon
questions.explanation: Split horizon prevents routing loops by not advertising routes back the direction they came from. Split horizon with poison reverse sends the route back with infinite metric (poison) instead.

questions.question: A help-desk admin uses a Windows-built-in graphical remote session protocol to access user workstations. The protocol encrypts the session and exposes the user's full desktop UI. Which TCP port is the default?
options: TCP 22 — SSH, not graphical RDP
TCP 5900 — VNC, not Microsoft RDP
TCP 443 — HTTPS, not RDP
TCP 3389
questions.explanation: RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) uses TCP/UDP port 3389 for Windows remote desktop connections. Exposing RDP directly to the internet is a major security risk — use VPN or RDP Gateway instead.

questions.question: A corporate browser is configured to send ALL outbound HTTP/HTTPS via an intermediary server on the corporate network. The intermediary CACHES popular content, FILTERS by category, ANONYMISES the client IP, and ENFORCES corporate policy (block, log). Which device is this?
options: A DHCP relay agent — forwards DHCP broadcasts between subnets on behalf of clients; does not cache content or filter outbound web traffic as an intermediary server
A proxy server
A router — forwards IP packets between networks at Layer 3; does not act as an intermediary server for HTTP/HTTPS or perform content caching and URL filtering
A bandwidth-monitoring tool (e.g., SNMP poller or MRTG) — passively collects traffic counters; does not intercept or filter web traffic as a server
questions.explanation: A proxy server handles requests on behalf of clients. Forward proxy: clients → proxy → internet (anonymization, filtering). Reverse proxy: internet → proxy → servers (load balancing, SSL termination).

questions.question: When a router needs to tell a sender 'destination unreachable', 'TTL exceeded' (used by traceroute), or to send a 'time exceeded' as part of a path-discovery, it does NOT use TCP or UDP — it uses a separate IP-layer message protocol. Which protocol?
options: ICMP
FTP — file transfer, not diagnostic
ICMP-misnamed crypto management — not a real protocol
RIP — routing protocol, not a diagnostic
questions.explanation: ICMP carries diagnostic and error messages between IP devices. Ping uses ICMP Echo Request/Reply. Traceroute sends packets with rising TTL values and reads ICMP Time Exceeded replies from each hop to map the path.

questions.question: Two large ISPs negotiate to exchange routes for hundreds of thousands of customer prefixes. The protocol carries an AS_PATH attribute, supports policy via communities + local-pref + MED, and is the only routing protocol that runs between distinct Autonomous Systems on the public internet. Which protocol?
options: An IGP for flat sites — wrong scope; IGPs run inside ONE AS, not between
BGP
Cisco-proprietary protocol — false; BGP is an open IETF standard
Distance-vector by hop count — false; BGP is path-vector with rich policy attributes
questions.explanation: BGP (EGP) manages routing between autonomous systems (AS numbers). It's used by ISPs to exchange routes on the internet and by enterprises with multiple ISP connections (multihoming). Path vector protocol.

questions.question: An 802.1Q trunk carries VLAN 10, 20, 30 with `switchport trunk native vlan 99` set. A frame arrives on the trunk WITHOUT an 802.1Q tag. Which VLAN does the switch assign to that untagged frame, and what's the requirement for the configuration?
options: The management VLAN — separate role; native VLAN is its own concept
Always VLAN 1 — false; native VLAN is configurable, defaults to 1 but can be any VLAN
Highest-utilised VLAN on the trunk — not how native VLAN works
The configured native VLAN (here 99)
questions.explanation: The native VLAN on a trunk receives untagged frames. Default is VLAN 1 on Cisco. If the native VLAN differs on each end of a trunk, traffic can hop VLANs (native VLAN mismatch attack vector).

questions.question: A switch port refuses to forward user traffic until the connected device PROVES its identity to a RADIUS server via EAP. Until authentication succeeds only EAPOL frames pass; after success the port opens to the user's data traffic (and may be dynamically placed in a VLAN). Which IEEE standard?
options: WPA3 — wireless encryption, not wired port auth
IEEE 802.3 auto-negotiation — speed/duplex, not authentication
IEEE 802.1X
IEEE 802.1Q — VLAN tagging, not authentication
questions.explanation: 802.1X (NAC) blocks all traffic on a port until the client authenticates via EAP (RADIUS). Used in enterprise wired and wireless networks to prevent unauthorized devices from accessing the network.

questions.question: A Cisco ACL line uses `permit ip 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 any`. The second value is the wildcard mask. Wildcard 0 means 'must match', wildcard 1 means 'don't care'. For the /24 network 10.0.0.0/24, the wildcard mask written explicitly is 0.0.0.255 — the INVERSE bit pattern of 255.255.255.0. Which describes a wildcard mask?
options: Inverse of a subnet mask — 0 bits MUST match, 1 bits are ignored (don't care)
Same as the subnet mask applied twice — false; a wildcard mask is the single bitwise inverse; you do not care about bits set to 1, and you must match bits set to 0
An IPv6-only construct with no wildcard bits in IPv4 ACLs — false; wildcard masks with "don't care" bits are standard in Cisco IPv4 ACLs
Identical to CIDR notation; a /24 prefix has a wildcard of 255.255.255.0 — false; in CIDR, /24 = subnet 255.255.255.0, so you care about the first 24 bits; the wildcard inverse is 0.0.0.255
questions.explanation: Wildcard masks are the bitwise inverse of subnet masks: subnet 255.255.255.0 → wildcard 0.0.0.255. Bits set to 0 must match the address exactly; bits set to 1 are wildcards. Used in IOS ACLs and OSPF network statements.

questions.question: An IP phone or wireless AP attached to a single Cat6 cable receives BOTH its Ethernet data AND its DC power over the same 4-pair cable from the switch port. The switch port (PSE) detects the device (PD), classifies its power class, and supplies up to 90 W (802.3bt). What is this technology called?
options: Power over Ethernet (PoE / 802.3af / at / bt)
Field cable certification — testing equipment specification, not power delivery
5-GHz wireless — wireless transmission, unrelated to wired PoE
100-Gbps Ethernet — high-speed standard, unrelated to PoE
questions.explanation: PoE (802.3af: 15.4W), PoE+ (802.3at: 30W), and PoE++ (802.3bt: 60-100W) power IP phones, wireless APs, IP cameras, and IoT devices through the network cable — no separate power outlet needed.

questions.question: An A record for `web.example.com → 203.0.113.42` is returned to a recursive resolver. The resolver CACHES the answer for a duration encoded in the response, then re-queries the authoritative when that timer expires. What's this caching timer called?
options: Maximum DNS response wait time — the resolver timeout before retrying or failing; not the duration that a cached record remains valid
DNS TTL (Time To Live) — how long a record may be cached before re-resolution
DHCP server lease duration — the time a client may use a DHCP-assigned IP address; unrelated to DNS record caching
Maximum recursive hop count — the number of referral steps a recursive resolver may follow before returning SERVFAIL; not the caching duration of a record
questions.explanation: DNS TTL controls caching duration. Low TTL (300s) = faster DNS changes propagate but more queries to your DNS server. High TTL (86400s = 24h) = efficient caching but slower change propagation.

questions.question: A laptop attached to a switch port sends 100 000 frames per second, each with a different RANDOM source MAC address. The switch's CAM table fills, evicts legitimate entries, and starts FLOODING traffic out every port (fail-open). The attacker then sniffs the flooded traffic. What's the attack name?
options: Malformed-BPDU STP attack — an attacker sends crafted BPDUs to take over the root bridge; the goal is topology manipulation, not CAM-table overflow flooding
CAM-table overflow / MAC flooding
Firmware corruption via malicious TFTP — a different attack class targeting software integrity, not CAM-table overflow or traffic flooding
CPU exhaustion — a control-plane attack targeting routing process or switch CPU; not a data-plane CAM-table overflow caused by MAC flooding
questions.explanation: When a switch's MAC table is full, it broadcasts frames out all ports (acts like a hub). An attacker runs macof or similar tool to flood the table, enabling passive interception of traffic.

questions.question: A protocol comparison: (A) establishes a connection via 3-way handshake, ACKs every segment, retransmits losses, orders bytes, performs flow + congestion control. (B) is fire-and-forget — sends datagrams with no handshake, no ACK, no retransmit, no ordering, low overhead. Which mapping?
options: TCP and UDP are interchangeable — false; TCP provides connection setup, ACKs, retransmits, and ordering guarantees while UDP is connectionless with none of these
TCP is always faster than UDP — false; UDP has lower per-packet overhead and lower latency precisely because it omits the connection, ACK, and retransmit mechanisms
TCP = connection-oriented with ACKs + ordering + retransmit +
UDP is more secure than TCP because it lacks the connection state that attackers can hijack — false; security is provided by upper-layer protocols (TLS, DTLS) regardless of TCP or UDP
questions.explanation: TCP is connection-oriented: three-way handshake, acknowledgements, ordering, retransmission, flow control — reliable but with overhead. UDP is connectionless and lightweight — low latency, no guarantees. TCP fits HTTP/SSH/SMTP; UDP fits DNS/VoIP/video streaming.

questions.question: A switch port runs 802.1X. When a user PC connects, the switch forwards the EAP exchange to a centralised server that (a) AUTHENTICATES the user / device against a directory, (b) AUTHORISES via attribute return (VLAN ID, downloadable ACL, session timeout), (c) ACCOUNTS by logging interim + stop records. Which server is this?
options: A router — L3 forwarder, not AAA
A perimeter firewall — packet inspection, not AAA
An authoritative DNS server — name resolution, not AAA
RADIUS
questions.explanation: RADIUS centralises AAA for network access. A switch, AP, or VPN concentrator (the RADIUS client) forwards user credentials to the RADIUS server, which validates them against an identity store (AD, LDAP). Used heavily by 802.1X.

questions.question: An enterprise places its public web + DNS + mail servers in a network segment with TWO firewalls bracketing it: one between internet and the segment, one between the segment and the internal LAN. Connections originate inbound from the internet to the segment; the segment cannot freely reach the LAN. What is this segment?
options: Disaster-recovery standby site — unrelated
Management VLAN — internal-admin scope, opposite shape
Guest Wi-Fi VLAN — isolated user network, different role
Screened subnet (DMZ)
questions.explanation: A true DMZ uses two firewalls: an outer firewall between internet and DMZ, and an inner firewall between DMZ and internal LAN. Servers in DMZ (web, mail, DNS) are accessible from the internet but isolated from internal network.

questions.question: A wireless designer walks a building with a spectrum analyser + heatmap tool to determine: best AP locations, channel plan to minimise CCI, required AP density for target client SNR. Output is a deployment plan + RF heat map. What is this activity called?
options: Site survey
Throughput speed test — post-deployment performance check, different activity
External security audit — policy/process, not RF
Inventory documentation — recording existing gear, not design
questions.explanation: Wireless site surveys (passive: listen, active: connect, predictive: software model) determine AP placement, channel assignments, power levels, and identify interference sources (microwaves, adjacent networks) before deployment.

questions.question: Classic Ethernet over a SHARED MEDIUM (10/100 Mbps half-duplex via a hub) uses an access-control rule: each NIC LISTENS for carrier before transmitting (CS), MANY can attempt (MA), and if two transmit simultaneously the collision is DETECTED (CD), each backs off a random time. What's this access method?
options: 802.11 wireless — that's CSMA/CA (Collision AVOIDANCE), different mechanism
Encryption algorithm — unrelated
Link-state routing protocol — unrelated
CSMA/CD
questions.explanation: CSMA/CD: Listen before transmitting (carrier sense). If collision detected, jam, then wait random backoff time. Only relevant for half-duplex Ethernet (hubs). Full-duplex switched networks don't use CSMA/CD.

questions.question: An NOC team is documenting their environment for a new on-call engineer. They produce a diagram showing routers, switches, firewalls, links, port assignments, and IP / VLAN labels — both physical patching AND logical L3 paths. What is this artefact called?
options: Application architecture diagram — software tiers, not network devices
HR organisation chart — people hierarchy, unrelated
Directory hierarchy diagram — AD users / OUs, unrelated
Network topology diagram
questions.explanation: Physical topology: actual cable/device layout. Logical topology: how data flows. Network diagrams help technicians understand the network, troubleshoot faster, and plan changes without disruption.

questions.question: Both routers and L3 switches forward IP packets at Layer 3. The KEY differences in practice: (a) L3 switches use specialised forwarding ASICs and are line-rate at LAN speeds with many ports, (b) Routers add WAN-protocol stacks (PPPoE, MPLS, ATM, NAT, QoS shaping). Which statement is correct?
options: Both forward L3

L3 switches can only terminate WAN circuits (PPPoE, MPLS); routers handle inter-VLAN Layer-3 forwarding in LAN environments — false; routers do WAN termination and L3 switches forward between VLANs at LAN speed
Routers always forward packets faster than L3 switches because they use purpose-built routing ASICs — false; L3 switches often use faster forwarding ASICs for LAN-speed inter-VLAN routing
L3 switches and routers are identical in all capabilities — false; routers support additional WAN protocol stacks that L3 switches typically lack
questions.explanation: Layer 3 switches forward between VLANs at near-wire speed using hardware ASICs — ideal for inter-VLAN routing on the LAN. Traditional routers add WAN circuits, NAT, complex routing policies, and VPN termination that L3 switches usually lack.

questions.question: A wireless engineer is upgrading APs from Wi-Fi 5 (802.11ac) to a newer standard. The newer standard is dual-band (2.4 + 5 GHz), uses OFDMA to schedule multiple clients within one channel time-slot, MU-MIMO uplink + downlink, BSS Coloring to reduce co-channel interference, and Target Wake Time for IoT battery life. Which standard?
options: 802.11n — older Wi-Fi 4, no OFDMA or BSS Coloring
Enterprise-only standard — licensing isn't gated this way
Wi-Fi 6 is 5-GHz-only — false; it's dual-band (6 GHz is Wi-Fi 6E)
questions.explanation: Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) improvements: OFDMA (divide channels for multiple users simultaneously), MU-MIMO 8x8, BSS Coloring (reduces interference), TWT (Target Wake Time for IoT battery life). Wi-Fi 6E adds 6 GHz band.

questions.question: A network IDS appliance inspects mirrored traffic. Its rule engine contains thousands of patterns that match BYTES, REGEX, OR protocol-state of known attacks (e.g., SQL injection strings, exploit-payload bytes, known malware C2 patterns). When a pattern matches, it raises an alert. What is each individual pattern called?
options: A firewall 5-tuple rule — different surface (L3/L4 ACL, not L7 byte pattern)
An X.509 certificate — TLS auth, unrelated
An IDS signature
A baseline — represents 'normal', not attack patterns
questions.explanation: IDS/IPS signatures are patterns matching known attack traffic (e.g., SQL injection string in HTTP, specific exploit payload). Signature-based detection is effective for known attacks but misses zero-days (needs anomaly detection).

questions.question: Authentication systems like Kerberos require all participants to have clocks within ~5 minutes of each other. Log correlation across servers requires consistent timestamps. A protocol distributes time hierarchically from a reference clock via UDP 123. Which protocol?
options: NTP
L2 topology discovery — LLDP / CDP, not time
Link-state routing protocol — OSPF, not time
IPsec key distribution — IKE, different surface
questions.explanation: NTP synchronizes device clocks to UTC. Critical for: log correlation (events must be in correct time sequence), Kerberos authentication (5-minute skew tolerance), certificate validation, and scheduled operations.

questions.question: An attacker on an access port crafts a DOUBLE-tagged frame (outer tag = the trunk's native VLAN, inner tag = the target VLAN). The first switch strips the outer tag (it matches the native VLAN) and forwards the still-tagged frame on the trunk. The second switch reads the inner tag and delivers the frame INTO a VLAN the attacker shouldn't reach. Which attack is this?
options: VLAN hopping (double-tagging)
Moving a user to a different VLAN at runtime — a normal administrative task; not a double-tagging attack or security exploit
High-availability replication of traffic across a standby switch — an HA mechanism, not a VLAN security attack involving double tags
WAN VLAN extension technology (VXLAN or MPLS-based L2VPN) — a legitimate service-provider transport mechanism, not an attacker technique using double-tagged frames
questions.explanation: VLAN hopping: (1) Switch spoofing — attacker's device negotiates a trunk with DTP; (2) Double tagging — attacker sends double-tagged frames to hop to native VLAN. Mitigation: disable DTP, change native VLAN from 1.

questions.question: A long inter-building data run is over 1 km. Copper UTP can't reach. The chosen medium uses LIGHT PULSES on glass strands, immune to EMI, and supports multi-km lengths at 10/40/100 Gbps with the right transceivers. What is it?
options: Coax — copper conductor with shielding, no light pulses, ≤ 500 m on legacy 10BASE5
Copper with fibre-mesh insulation — not a real cable type
Wireless point-to-point — useful but susceptible to weather/LoS
Fibre optic
questions.explanation: Fiber optic cabling is immune to electromagnetic interference, carries far more bandwidth than copper, reaches much greater distances (single-mode up to ~80 km, multi-mode up to ~2 km), and emits no electrical signal that can be tapped passively.

questions.question: An optical engineer compares two fibre flavours: (A) tiny ~9 µm core, ONE light path, used for inter-DC and metro links up to tens of km. (B) larger ~50-62.5 µm core, MULTIPLE light paths with modal dispersion, used for intra-DC under ~500 m at 10 Gbps. Which mapping?
options: Multi-mode fiber is always faster than single-mode — false; single-mode supports higher data rates over longer paths because it uses a laser with a single light path
Single-mode: one light path, longer reach (km)
Only multi-mode fiber supports Ethernet standards — false; both single-mode and multi-mode fiber carry Ethernet (10GBase-SR, 10GBase-LR, etc.) over different light path designs
Single-mode fiber is used for short runs under 100 m because its narrow core limits the light path — false; single-mode fiber is used for long-reach paths; multi-mode is the short-run standard
questions.explanation: Single-mode fiber has an 8-10 µm core, uses a laser source, and supports long reach (km). Multi-mode has a 50/62.5 µm core, uses LED/VCSEL sources, and is limited to roughly 2 km because modal dispersion broadens the pulse over distance.

questions.question: A DHCP server hands out an IP for a finite TIME (T). At 50% (T/2) the client UNICASTS a renewal to the same server. At ~87.5% (T2) the client BROADCASTS a rebind in case the original server is gone. If neither succeeds before expiry, the client RELEASES the address. What's this lifecycle called?
options: DHCP lease lifecycle — temporary assignment with T1 (50% renewal) and T2 (~87.5% rebind) timers
Static IP reservation — a permanent server-side assignment with no lifecycle timers; the client never unicasts a renewal or broadcasts a rebind request
DHCP addresses never expire — false; DHCP leases are time-bounded; the lifecycle includes T1 renewal, T2 rebind, and expiry stages
The lease survives reboots and NIC changes indefinitely — false; a client reboot re-runs the DORA sequence and a NIC change presents a new MAC, triggering a new lease lifecycle
questions.explanation: DHCP leases are temporary. At 50% expiry, client sends unicast renewal to original server. At 87.5%, broadcasts rebind request to any server. If no response, IP expires and client starts DORA process again.

questions.question: The OSI layer at the BOTTOM of the stack transmits raw bits over a physical medium. It defines voltage levels (copper), light pulses (fibre), radio carriers (wireless), connectors (RJ-45, LC), and bit-clock encoding (NRZ, PAM4). Which layer?
options: OSI Physical Layer (Layer 1)
OSI Network Layer (Layer 3) — defines logical IP addressing and packet routing; not the layer that specifies physical connectors, voltage levels, or bit encoding
OSI Data Link Layer (Layer 2) — defines frame structure, MAC addresses, and error detection; not the layer that specifies physical medium, connector types, or bit-clock encoding
OSI Transport Layer (Layer 4) — defines TCP/UDP port numbers and end-to-end segment delivery; not the layer that specifies physical cable types or signal encoding
questions.explanation: Layer 1 (Physical) deals with: bit encoding, voltage levels, cable specs (Cat6, fiber), connectors (RJ45, LC, SC), transmission rates, and synchronization. Devices: hubs, repeaters, cabling. No addressing.

questions.question: An enterprise wants ONE central system for: (a) IPv4/IPv6 address space planning + allocation, (b) DHCP scope management, (c) DNS zone management, (d) per-IP audit trail. Vendors include Infoblox, BlueCat, Solarwinds. What's this category of system?
options: Network-monitoring system — polls SNMP counters for performance management; does not manage IP address space, DHCP scopes, or provide a per-IP audit trail
IP Address Management (IPAM) — manages IP space + DHCP + DNS + audit centrally
Network Access Control — provides device posture management and quarantine; does not manage IP address allocation, DHCP, or DNS zone administration
A link-state routing protocol — provides topology management and IP reachability for routers; not a system for tracking IP address space or managing DHCP/DNS services
questions.explanation: IPAM tools (Windows Server IPAM, phpIPAM, Infoblox) provide visibility into IP address utilization, prevent conflicts, manage DHCP scopes, and integrate with DNS. Critical for large networks to avoid IP chaos.

questions.question: An IPv4 Class B network uses the FIRST 16 bits for the network portion (per the legacy classful scheme). The DEFAULT subnet mask matches those 16 bits as 1s. Which mask?
options: 255.255.255.128 — that's /25, not Class B default
255.0.0.0 — that's /8, the Class A default
255.255.255.0 — that's /24, the Class C default
questions.explanation: Class B (128.0.0.0–191.255.255.255) has a default mask of 255.255.0.0 (/16), providing 16 bits for hosts (65,534 usable). Class A = 255.0.0.0 (/8), Class C = 255.255.255.0 (/24).

questions.question: An L2 segment with multiple redundant inter-switch links must avoid endless frame circulation. Without intervention a broadcast frame would be flooded forever, multiplying at each switch. A protocol elects a root, calculates least-cost paths, and BLOCKS the redundant ports — preserving a loop-free active topology. Which?
options: A BGP routing loop — different layer (L3 inter-AS, not L2 broadcast)
A DNS resolution loop — different surface entirely
L2 loop
BGP AS_PATH loop detection — L3 inter-AS, not L2 broadcast loops
questions.explanation: Layer 2 loops: frames have no TTL (unlike IP), so looping frames multiply exponentially causing broadcast storms. STP (802.1D) selects a root bridge and blocks redundant paths, creating a loop-free tree topology.

questions.question: A network operator needs to manage routers and switches even when the data network is DOWN (firmware push, recovery, config rollback). A separate physical path via console servers + dedicated mgmt NICs sits on a completely separate set of cables. What's this management path called?
options: Out-of-band management
Reused corporate internet via VPN — that's in-band, fails if internet fails
VLAN 1 as management VLAN — in-band, fails with the data plane
Wireless backup network — in-band, depends on the data network
questions.explanation: OOB management uses separate physical connectivity (dedicated management ports, cellular modems, console servers). Critical for restoring failed devices when production network is unavailable.

questions.question: An enterprise wants every device that joins the LAN (wired OR Wi-Fi) to be checked: domain-joined? AV running and current? OS patches up to date? If yes, place in production VLAN; if no, quarantine VLAN with limited remediation access. Which system class enforces this?
options: Physical-access badge system — building security, not network access
Network Access Control (NAC)
Perimeter firewall — packet inspection, not host posture
Site-to-site VPN — connectivity, not posture-based admission
questions.explanation: NAC (Cisco ISE, Aruba ClearPass, Forescout) enforces posture assessment before allowing devices on the network. Can place non-compliant or unknown devices in quarantine VLANs for remediation.

questions.question: An FTP client uploads files to a corporate file server. Capture shows the login (USER + PASS) and every file's bytes traversing the network IN PLAINTEXT. Which ports does FTP use and why is it considered insecure?
options: Port 443 (HTTPS) — false; FTP doesn't use 443
Port 22 (SSH) — false; that's SFTP/SCP, not classic FTP
Port 80 (HTTP-style) — false; FTP has its own ports
TCP 21 (control) + 20 (active-data)
questions.explanation: FTP uses port 21 for the control channel and port 20 for the active-mode data channel; passive mode uses an ephemeral data port. Credentials and payload travel in cleartext, so prefer SFTP (over SSH/22) or FTPS (FTP wrapped in TLS).

questions.question: Two routers terminate a GRE tunnel for non-IP-encapsulated traffic. The underlying transport has no inherent reachability detection — so a one-way break leaves the tunnel 'up' even though traffic is black-holed. A feature periodically probes the remote end and brings the tunnel interface down if probes fail. Which feature?
options: GRE signature authentication — different (security)
IPComp compression — different (efficiency)
IPsec transport-mode wrapping — different (security)
GRE keepalive
questions.explanation: GRE keepalives detect when the remote tunnel endpoint is unreachable (even if the physical interface is up). Without keepalives, the tunnel interface stays up and routing protocols don't detect the failure. Configured with 'tunnel keepalive'.

questions.question: An installer terminating RJ-45 jacks must choose a pinout. The two standardised orderings are T568A and T568B. A STRAIGHT-THROUGH patch cable uses the SAME standard on both ends; a CROSSOVER cable uses ONE end with each standard (one T568A, the other T568B). Which statement is correct?
options: T568A and T568B are TIA/EIA pinouts for RJ-45
T568B gives higher throughput on Cat 6 — false; both deliver identical throughput when terminated consistently
T568A is for fibre connectors — false; T568A/B are 8-pin RJ-45 copper standards
T568A is Cat5e and T568B is Cat6 — false; both pinouts apply to both categories
questions.explanation: Both 568A and 568B are valid. Organizations standardize on one (most use 568B). Straight-through: same standard both ends — connects PC to switch. Crossover: 568A one end, 568B the other — connects PC to PC or switch to switch (modern NICs auto-MDIX makes crossovers unnecessary).

questions.question: A DHCP server allocates IPs to clients. Each allocation has a TIME-bound contract: client may KEEP the IP for that long, then must renew or release. Operationally: short for guest Wi-Fi (8 h), longer for servers (days/weeks). Which DHCP parameter does this?
options: Maximum clients per DHCP server — a capacity limit that controls how many clients can register at one time, not the duration each allocation remains valid
DHCP OFFER response time — the latency from client request to server response; not the parameter controlling how long each allocated IP remains valid
DORA replay resistance — a security property preventing replay attacks against the four-step exchange; not a parameter controlling allocation duration or renewal time
DHCP lease time
questions.explanation: Short lease (1-2 hours): for guest/public Wi-Fi where devices come and go. Long lease (8 days): for corporate servers with stable IPs. Too-short leases cause excessive DHCP traffic; too-long can exhaust pools.

questions.question: An NOC routes log events from routers, switches, firewalls, and Linux servers to a central log server using UDP/TCP 514. Each event carries a severity code 0-7. Which describes the system + the severity scale?
options: Central syslog server
Application performance monitor (APM) — traces transaction response times and user experience metrics; not a central log aggregation server using syslog protocol
SNMP manager polling counters — queries MIBs via UDP 161 to collect interface and resource statistics; not a central syslog server receiving event streams on UDP/TCP 514
Firewall-only log aggregator — a device-specific log store; a central syslog server receives events from routers, switches, firewalls, and Linux servers simultaneously
questions.explanation: Syslog (UDP 514, TCP 6514 for TLS) forwards device logs to a central server. Common mnemonic: Every Awful Crisis Eventually Will Neglect Innocent Demons. Level 3 and above warrant immediate investigation.

questions.question: A flat L2 segment with multiple inter-switch links AND no STP suddenly sees traffic on every port spiking to 100% utilisation. Every broadcast loops forever, multiplying in volume. Ping packets reach 100% loss. What's happening?
options: Unusual unicast traffic spike from a single host — would not cause broadcasts to multiply and flood every port across multiple switches
A network loop is multiplying broadcasts/floods exponentially because STP is missing or broken
Volumetric DDoS attack from an external source — would create directional congestion on the uplink but would not cause L2 broadcasts to loop and multiply exponentially
IPTV multicast spike — typically contained by IGMP snooping on switches; would not produce the looping, multiplying broadcast storm pattern seen when STP is absent
questions.explanation: Broadcast storms occur when Ethernet frames loop between switches. Without STP, a single loop causes exponential frame multiplication. Symptoms: 100% link utilization, switch CPU at max, network unresponsive. STP prevents this.

questions.question: A pair of Ethernet hosts on a SHARED hub run half-duplex and use CSMA/CD; each collision triggers backoff. A pair of Ethernet hosts on a SWITCH port pair run full-duplex; TX and RX are on separate pairs and collisions are physically impossible. Which statement reflects this?
options: Half-duplex and full-duplex produce the same collision rate on a shared medium — false; full-duplex eliminates collisions entirely while half-duplex relies on CSMA/CD to detect and recover from them

Collisions only occur on fibre-optic Ethernet links because copper pairs share a common medium — false; collisions occur on any half-duplex shared medium regardless of cable type; CSMA/CD handles them
Half-duplex uses CSMA/CD to recover from collisions

Full-duplex has more collisions than half-duplex because both TX and RX are active simultaneously — false; full-duplex dedicated TX/RX pairs make collisions physically impossible, eliminating the need for CSMA/CD
questions.explanation: In half-duplex (hubs), only one device sends at a time; collisions trigger backoff/retransmit. In full-duplex (switches), dedicated TX/RX pairs prevent collisions entirely — CSMA/CD is disabled for better performance.

questions.question: An ISP wants to advertise ONE prefix that covers FOUR contiguous /24 customer networks (203.0.113.0/24, 203.0.114.0/24, 203.0.115.0/24, 203.0.116.0/24 — wait, only 113-116 are contiguous if aligned). Combining contiguous blocks into one larger prefix to shrink the routing table is called what?
options: Supernetting / CIDR aggregation
Subnetting — splits a classful network into smaller pieces; the OPPOSITE direction
VXLAN stretched VLAN — L2 extension, different concept
Firewall rule grouping — security policy organisation, not routing aggregation
questions.explanation: Supernetting (route aggregation) advertises multiple contiguous networks as one summary route — reduces routing table size on internet-facing routers. ISPs aggregate customer prefixes; enterprises aggregate branch routes.

questions.question: Two acronyms both abbreviate to 'TTL' but mean different things: (A) in a DNS record — a CACHING duration in seconds at the resolver. (B) in an IP packet header — a HOP COUNT decremented by each router that drops the packet at 0. Which is which?
options: IP TTL counted in seconds — false; it's hop count
DNS TTL is router hops — false; DNS TTL is seconds
DNS TTL = cache lifetime in seconds
Identical mechanism — false
questions.explanation: DNS TTL controls cache duration (low=fast propagation, high=efficient). IP TTL (IPv4)/Hop Limit (IPv6) prevents infinite routing loops — each router decrements by 1. Different concepts that happen to share a name.

questions.question: An IP phone vendor's datasheet lists PoE classes: 802.3af up to 15.4 W per port, 802.3at up to 30 W, 802.3bt up to 60 / 90 W per port (Type 3 / 4). What family of IEEE standards does this describe?
options: Ethernet speed standards (10/100/1000/10G) — different family (802.3 speed)
VLAN-tagging extensions (802.1Q / ad) — wrong family
Wireless enterprise auth — wrong family entirely
questions.explanation: PoE standards deliver power and data over Ethernet. 802.3af: basic PoE for IP phones, small APs. 802.3at: PoE+ for PTZ cameras, tablets. 802.3bt: PoE++ for laptops, multi-radio APs, smart lighting systems.

questions.question: A network team produces TWO complementary diagrams for an audit: (1) LOGICAL — IP / VLAN / routing relationships, ignoring physical placement. (2) PHYSICAL — device location, rack-units, cable patching, IDF/MDF wiring. Which describes the two diagram types?
options: Only the physical diagram matters for audits — false; logical diagrams showing IP addressing, VLAN layout, and routing relationships are equally essential
Network diagrams are only useful during outages — false; baseline logical and physical documentation is required for change management, audits, and troubleshooting at any time
Logical: IPs, VLANs, routing
Diagrams are unnecessary for small networks — false; even small networks benefit from both logical (IP, routing) and physical (rack, cable) documentation
questions.explanation: Good network documentation combines a logical diagram (IP addressing, VLAN map, routing) with a physical diagram (device locations, cable runs, rack layout). Both are essential for planning, change management, and rapid troubleshooting.

questions.question: A pentester runs reconnaissance with an open-source TCP/IP port scanner. Common scan types: `-sn` (ping sweep), `-sS` (TCP SYN half-open), `-sV` (version detection), `-sU` (UDP scan), `-A` (aggressive: OS detection + version + scripts + traceroute). Which tool?
options: Firewall-management GUI — not a scanner
Wireshark / tshark — passive capture, not active scanning
Nmap
SNMP-poll dashboard — passive polling, not active scanning
questions.explanation: Nmap is the standard network reconnaissance tool. Common uses: discover live hosts, enumerate open ports, detect service versions, identify OS. Use with permission only — unauthorized scanning is illegal in many jurisdictions.

questions.question: A NAS / iSCSI / NFS storage VLAN configures its NICs and switches for an Ethernet payload SIZE of 9000 bytes (above the standard 1500). Throughput per packet rises; per-byte CPU overhead falls. Senders and receivers must both support the larger MTU. What's this called?
options: Jumbo frames
Wireless mesh — unrelated
Runt/giant error counter — different concept (oversized errors)
Fragmented Ethernet — fragmentation is a different mechanism that operates ABOVE Ethernet (IP fragmentation)
questions.explanation: Jumbo frames require all devices in the path to support the larger MTU — switch, NIC, and any intermediate devices. If one device doesn't support jumbo frames, traffic drops (MTU mismatch). Enable per-interface, ensure end-to-end consistency.

questions.question: Two OSPF routers on the same Ethernet broadcast segment exchange Hello packets to discover each other and verify the neighbour is still alive. Defaults: Hello every 10 s, Dead 4× the Hello (40 s). If either side has different timer values, no adjacency forms. What is the purpose of these timers?
options: Hello = keepalive interval (10 s default)
Hello + Dead compute the route metric — false; metric is cost (interface-bandwidth based)
Hello + Dead encrypt OSPF messages — false; encryption is separate (MD5/HMAC-SHA option)
Hello + Dead define OSPF areas — false; area is a config parameter, not derived from timers
questions.explanation: OSPF Hello and Dead intervals must match between neighbors. Default: Hello=10s, Dead=40s on Ethernet. Mismatch = no adjacency. Lower timers = faster failure detection but more CPU/bandwidth. Never-match is a common misconfiguration.

questions.question: A service-provider backbone needs to carry the customer's 802.1Q-tagged VLANs across the SP core WITHOUT renumbering them. The SP wraps the customer frame in a SECOND 802.1Q tag (the S-Tag) before transmitting on the SP core; pops it on egress. What is this technology called?
options: 802.1X — port-based network access control for authenticating devices on a LAN; a different IEEE standard, not a provider VLAN encapsulation technique
802.1ad / Q-in-Q (provider bridging)
IPsec double-encryption mode — encrypts data twice using nested security associations; a security mechanism unrelated to provider VLAN stacking
First-hop redundancy protocol (HSRP or VRRP) — provides gateway failover for end hosts; a different concept unrelated to provider VLAN transport
questions.explanation: QinQ encapsulates customer 802.1Q frames inside a provider S-Tag (outer VLAN). Customer can use any VLAN IDs (1-4094) — the provider only sees the outer S-Tag. Common in metro Ethernet and ISP aggregation networks.

questions.question: A branch router has specific routes for the local subnets and a CATCH-ALL route for anything else, pointing at the WAN edge: `ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.1`. Any packet that doesn't match a more specific entry follows this route. What is it called?
options: OSPF `default-information originate` — propagates a default into OSPF, related but a different mechanism
Loopback /32 route — describes the router's local loopback, not the catch-all
Default route (0.0.0.0/0)
Static /32 host route — points at a single host, not a catch-all
questions.explanation: The default route (0.0.0.0/0) is the least specific route — matches everything. Routers apply longest prefix match: /32 > /24 > /16 > /0. The default route catches all traffic with no more-specific match and forwards it upstream.

questions.question: After a topology change (link drop, new neighbour) every router in an OSPF area must (a) detect the event, (b) recompute its SPF tree, (c) install new RIB/FIB entries, (d) the network stabilises. The total wall-clock duration is what's measured. What's this period called?
options: DHCP DORA exchange time — the four-step IP address assignment sequence; a different process unrelated to routing-protocol network convergence
NTP clock synchronisation time — the duration for clocks to align to a reference; unrelated to network routing-table convergence after a topology change
Physical deployment time — the time to rack and cable a new device; not a measure of routing-protocol network state stabilisation
Network convergence time
questions.explanation: Convergence: OSPF typically converges in seconds (SPF delay); EIGRP can converge in milliseconds (DUAL with feasible successors). BGP is slow (minutes for full internet convergence). During convergence, packets may be dropped or loop.

questions.question: A SOC team compares two defensive surfaces: (A) Passively MONITORS network traffic against a signature database; alerts on a match; does NOT engage attackers. (B) Looks like a vulnerable system, has NO real production data, EXISTS to ATTRACT attacker activity and log their tradecraft. Which is which?
options: IDS = passive alerts on known attack patterns
A honeypot is always a physical hardware server placed in the DMZ — false; many honeypots are virtualised software instances and are not restricted to a physical deployment
An IDS automatically blocks matched traffic and generates alerts — false; blocking is the role of an IPS; an IDS passively monitors and generates alerts without inline enforcement
IDS and honeypot serve identical defensive roles — false; an IDS generates alerts on real production traffic while a honeypot attracts attackers to a fake system to study their techniques
questions.explanation: IDS (Intrusion Detection System): monitors real production traffic for attacks. Honeypot: fake vulnerable system to lure attackers away from real assets and study their methods. Both are complementary security controls.

questions.question: An NTP client queries a peer that lists itself as Stratum 2 in its packets. The peer is two hops away (in NTP terms) from a primary reference clock (Stratum 1, e.g. a GPS-synced atomic clock = Stratum 0). What does the stratum number represent?
options: Hop-distance from a Stratum 0 reference clock
An authentication strength tier indicating how many factors the NTP clock source requires — not what the stratum number measures in the NTP hierarchy
The NTP software version running on the queried time server — not what stratum means; stratum indicates hop distance from a reference clock, not software version
A key-authentication level controlling which NTP peers are trusted — not what stratum means; stratum measures distance from the reference clock, not authentication credential strength
questions.explanation: NTP stratum is the distance, in hops, from a Stratum-0 reference clock such as a GPS or atomic source. Stratum 1 servers are directly attached to that reference; Stratum 2 syncs from Stratum 1, and so on. Stratum 16 means unsynchronised.

questions.question: A company runs `example.com` both publicly (web pages for the world) AND on its internal network (`intranet.example.com` resolves to an RFC1918 IP only inside the corporate network). The SAME domain returns DIFFERENT records depending on whether the query came from inside or outside. What's this technique called?
options: DNS failover rewriting — different concept
DNSSEC signed zones — orthogonal (integrity, not view selection)
Long-TTL caching — different concept
Split DNS (split-horizon DNS)
questions.explanation: Split DNS runs separate zone files for internal/external. 'corp.example.com' resolves to 10.1.1.100 internally (direct access) vs 203.0.113.5 externally (through load balancer/WAF). Hides internal IP schema from internet.

questions.question: A SOC engineer wants to feed a copy of all traffic between two specific switch ports to an IDS appliance on a third port — without disrupting production. The switch copies inbound + outbound frames from the SOURCE port(s) and emits them on the MONITOR port. What's this switch feature called?
options: VLAN ID reuse — different feature
MAC port-security — different feature (port-level MAC limit)
Link aggregation (LAG / EtherChannel) — different feature (bundling)
Port mirroring / SPAN
questions.explanation: SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) mirrors traffic to an analysis port. Local SPAN: same switch. RSPAN: across switches via a RSPAN VLAN. ERSPAN: over GRE tunnel to a remote analyzer. Used for IDS, packet capture, performance monitoring.

questions.question: A global enterprise wants to consolidate SD-WAN, Secure Web Gateway (SWG), CASB, ZTNA, and Firewall-as-a-Service into a single cloud-delivered framework to replace its hub-and-spoke MPLS + on-prem security stack. Which architecture fits this requirement?
options: Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) cloud-delivered model
Traditional site-to-site IPsec VPN mesh — provides secure encrypted tunnels between fixed sites but does not include cloud-delivered SWG, CASB, ZTNA, or FWaaS
MPLS with a centralised on-premises next-generation secure firewall stack — consolidates security inspection on-premises; not a cloud-delivered converged edge model
Layer 2 VPN over carrier Ethernet (VPLS or EVPN) — a WAN transport service; it provides connectivity but no cloud-delivered secure web gateway or access-security functions
questions.explanation: SASE (Secure Access Service Edge) converges networking (SD-WAN) and security services (SWG, CASB, ZTNA, FWaaS) into a single cloud-delivered model, eliminating backhaul to a central data center.

questions.question: In a Software-Defined Networking (SDN) architecture, a centralized controller programs forwarding rules into switches using OpenFlow. Which statement correctly describes the control plane vs data plane separation?
options: Controller runs the control plane; switches forward in the data plane
Control and data planes are merged on each switch with no central controller
The data plane runs on the controller while switches only provide ports
Switches run both control and data planes locally; controller just monitors
questions.explanation: SDN separates the control plane (the centralised controller making forwarding decisions) from the data plane (switches that forward packets). The controller installs flow rules southbound via OpenFlow, while applications consume the controller via northbound APIs.

questions.question: A retail chain with 200 branches uses SD-WAN to combine broadband, LTE, and MPLS links. Real-time voice should always take the lowest-latency path while bulk backups should use the cheapest link. Which SD-WAN capability enables this?
options: Application-aware dynamic path selection based on real-time SLA
Static DSCP marking applied only at the access-layer switch — assigns a fixed quality marking at ingress but does not dynamically select a path based on real-time SLA metrics
Static routing tuned per route using administrative distance — a fixed preference mechanism that does not dynamically adapt path selection to real-time latency or jitter conditions
Spanning Tree Protocol port cost set lower on the preferred uplink — an L2 loop-prevention mechanism that selects a forwarding path based on cost, not real-time SLA measurements
questions.explanation: SD-WAN performs dynamic path selection per application by continuously measuring link SLA metrics (latency, jitter, loss) and steering traffic accordingly. It is transport-agnostic and managed via a centralized policy controller.

questions.question: A security team wants to replace the legacy remote-access VPN (which gives users broad network access) with a model that grants per-application access based on user identity and device posture, with implicit deny by default. Which solution matches?
options: GRE tunnel with IPsec transport-mode encryption — a network-level tunnel that extends Layer 3 connectivity between sites; it grants network-level access, not per-application brokered access
Split-tunnel SSL VPN with full subnet routes pushed to clients — grants access to whole network subnets rather than per-application brokered sessions with implicit deny
Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) per-application brokered model
IPsec site-to-site VPN with pre-shared keys — provides network-level connectivity between fixed locations; it does not implement a per-application zero-trust access model
questions.explanation: ZTNA enforces identity- and context-based access to individual applications (not whole subnets), with implicit deny. Traditional VPNs typically grant broad lateral network access once authenticated.

questions.question: A data center fabric needs to support more than 4,096 logical Layer 2 segments over a routed IP underlay. The overlay uses UDP port 4789 and a 24-bit segment identifier. Which technology is being described?
options: VXLAN
802.1Q VLAN trunking
GRE with Layer 2 payload
MPLS L2VPN
questions.explanation: VXLAN encapsulates Ethernet frames in UDP (port 4789) and uses a 24-bit VNI, allowing over 16 million segments versus the 12-bit (4,094 usable) VLAN ID limit. It creates Layer 2 overlays across a Layer 3 underlay.

questions.question: An architect needs a dedicated, private, high-bandwidth link from on-premises to AWS with consistent low latency (bypassing the public internet) for a 10 Gbps workload. Which option is best?
options: Site-to-site IPsec VPN over the public internet — an encrypted tunnel but traverses the shared public internet, not a dedicated private circuit with predictable latency
AWS NAT Gateway fronted by an Elastic IP — provides outbound internet access for private subnets; not a dedicated private circuit to on-premises
AWS Direct Connect dedicated private circuit
Transit Gateway attachment over public endpoints — routes traffic between VPCs and on-premises over the public internet by default, not a dedicated private connection
questions.explanation: AWS Direct Connect (like Azure ExpressRoute and GCP Cloud Interconnect) provides a dedicated private circuit with predictable bandwidth and latency. IPsec VPNs traverse the public internet and are limited by internet congestion.

questions.question: A network engineer enables IPv6 on a LAN. Hosts must auto-configure their own addresses from the router's advertised /64 prefix without requiring a stateful server to assign them. Which mechanism accomplishes this?
options: Static manual addressing using EUI-64 host suffixes — requires an administrator to configure each host address manually; not an automatic mechanism driven by router advertisements
SLAAC with Router Advertisements from the gateway
DHCPv6 stateful mode with a managed address pool — uses a dedicated DHCPv6 server to assign addresses; not a stateless mechanism built from the router-advertised prefix
NAT64/DNS64 translation gateway — enables IPv6-only hosts to reach IPv4 destinations; not a mechanism for hosts to auto-configure addresses from router-advertised prefixes
questions.explanation: SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) lets hosts build their own IPv6 address from the /64 prefix in a Router Advertisement (RA) plus an interface identifier. DHCPv6 stateful mode requires a server to track and assign addresses.

questions.question: A university upgrades its lecture halls from 802.11ac to 802.11ax to support hundreds of concurrent clients per AP. Which Wi-Fi 6 feature most directly improves performance in high-density deployments by allowing a single transmission to serve multiple clients simultaneously on different subcarriers?
options: MU-MIMO downlink only — sends spatial streams to multiple clients at once
Channel bonding up to 160 MHz — widens the channel for raw bandwidth gains
OFDMA — subdivides a channel into Resource Units so one TX serves many clients
Dynamic Frequency Selection (DFS) — avoids radar bands by choosing channels
questions.explanation: OFDMA subdivides a channel into Resource Units so one transmission can serve multiple clients at once. Combined with BSS coloring, TWT, and 1024-QAM, it drastically improves efficiency in dense environments.

questions.question: After a DNS cache poisoning incident, a company wants cryptographic guarantees that resolved records have not been tampered with and truly come from the authoritative zone. Which technology should be enabled?
options: Round-robin DNS with TTL set to zero — distributes load across multiple records and prevents caching but provides no cryptographic guarantee that records have not been tampered with
Split-horizon DNS for internal users — returns different records to internal vs external resolvers; does not sign or cryptographically verify the integrity of those records
DNSSEC with RRSIG and DNSKEY records
DNS over HTTPS (DoH) on resolvers only — encrypts the DNS transport channel between client and resolver but does not cryptographically sign or validate the authoritative records themselves
questions.explanation: DNSSEC signs zone records with private keys; resolvers validate the RRSIG signatures using the published DNSKEY, ensuring integrity and authenticity of responses. DoH encrypts the query channel but does not authenticate record data.

questions.question: A technician must locate a break in a multi-kilometer single-mode fiber run and identify the exact distance to the fault from the patch panel. Which tool is appropriate?
options: Cable certifier for Cat 6A copper — measures NEXT, insertion loss, and return loss on twisted-pair copper; not designed to locate faults or measure distance in fiber runs
Wi-Fi spectrum analyser — visualises 2.4/5/6-GHz RF channel utilisation; not a tool for locating breaks in a fiber run or measuring fault distance
Tone generator and inductive probe — traces copper cable runs at a patch panel; not suitable for locating breaks or measuring distance to faults in multi-kilometer fiber
Optical Time Domain Reflectometer (OTDR) — locates fiber faults by distance
questions.explanation: An OTDR sends optical pulses down a fiber and measures back-scattered light to pinpoint the distance to breaks, bends, and splices. A TDR performs the same function for copper cabling. Tone generators only help trace runs, not locate faults with distance precision.

questions.question: A network engineer is comparing routing-protocol categories. Link-state protocols build a topology database via LSAs and run a shortest-path algorithm on the graph. Distance-vector protocols exchange routing-table summaries with neighbours and run Bellman-Ford-style updates. Which TWO are link-state protocols?
options: OSPF — classic IETF link-state IGP, uses LSAs and Dijkstra SPF
IS-IS — ISO link-state IGP, widely used in service-provider cores, also runs Dijkstra over a link-state database
RIP — a classic distance-vector protocol that exchanges full routing-table hop-count summaries with neighbours; it does not flood LSAs or run a shortest-path algorithm
EIGRP — Cisco advanced distance-vector protocol using the DUAL algorithm; it does not build an LSA-based topology database or run Dijkstra SPF
questions.explanation: OSPF and IS-IS both flood link-state advertisements and run Dijkstra's SPF. RIP is distance-vector (hop count). BGP is a path-vector protocol — it tracks the AS path, not link-state.
